“You haven't been in Bath long enough,” he said, “to enjoy its evening gatherings.”

“Oh, no. The usual kind has no appeal for me. I don't play cards.”

“You didn't before, I know. You never used to like them, but time changes many things.”

“I haven't changed that much yet,” Anne exclaimed, then stopped, afraid of some misunderstanding she could scarcely define. After a few moments he said, apparently carried by a sudden feeling, “It is a long time, certainly. Eight and a half years is a long time.”

Whether he might have said more was a question Anne's imagination would have to consider in a quieter moment. While his words were still in her ears, Henrietta abruptly drew her attention elsewhere. Eager to use this opportunity to go out, she urged her companions to hurry before anyone else arrived.

They had to move. Anne declared herself quite ready and tried to appear so. Yet she felt that, if Henrietta could have known the regret and reluctance with which she left that chair and prepared to leave the room, her own feelings for her cousin, and the very certainty that he loved her, would have given her reason to pity Anne.

Their preparations were suddenly interrupted. They heard the alarming sounds of more visitors approaching, and the door opened to admit Sir Walter and Miss Elliot. Their entrance seemed to chill everyone. Anne immediately felt oppressed, and everywhere she looked she saw signs of the same response. The room's warmth, freedom, and good humor vanished, replaced by cold self-possession, determined silence, or empty conversation to match her father and sister's heartless elegance. How humiliating it was to recognize this!

Her watchful concern was satisfied on one point. Both acknowledged Captain Wentworth again, and Elizabeth did so more pleasantly than before. She even spoke to him once and looked his way several times. Elizabeth was, in fact, considering a significant step, as events soon made clear. After wasting a few minutes on the expected meaningless remarks, she began issuing the invitation that would settle all her remaining social obligations to the Musgroves. “Tomorrow evening, to meet a few friends; nothing formal.” She delivered it all with considerable grace. The cards she had brought, announcing “Miss Elliot at home,” were placed on the table with a courteous smile embracing everyone, while one smile and one card were directed more particularly at Captain Wentworth. The truth was that Elizabeth had spent enough time in Bath to appreciate the value of a man with his bearing and appearance.

“They ought to concern you, Dorian. Every gentleman cares about his reputation. You don't want people to describe you as someone filthy and corrupt. Of course you have your social standing, your money, and all the rest. But wealth and rank aren't everything. Understand, I don't believe these rumors. At least, when I look at you, I cannot believe them. Sin leaves its marks on a man's face. It cannot stay hidden. People sometimes speak of secret vices, but there is no such thing. If a man has a shameful habit, you see it in the lines around his mouth, in his drooping eyelids, even in the shape of his hands. Last year someone came to ask me to paint his portrait. I won't give his name, but you know him. I had never seen him before, and at that time I had heard nothing about him, though I have heard plenty since. He offered me an enormous sum. I turned him down. There was something about the shape of his fingers that repelled me. I now know that my impression of him was entirely right. He leads a terrible life. But your face, Dorian, looks so pure, so bright and innocent, and your wonderful youth seems untouched by trouble. I cannot believe anything bad about you. Yet I hardly see you, and you never visit the studio anymore. When we are apart and I hear the awful things people whisper about you, I don't know how to answer. Why does a man like the Duke of Berwick leave a room at his club when you walk in? Why do so many gentlemen in London refuse to visit your house or welcome you into theirs? You were once friends with Lord Staveley. I saw him at dinner last week. Your name came up when we were discussing the miniature paintings you lent to the exhibition at the Dudley. Staveley sneered and said that you might have excellent artistic taste, but no innocent girl should be allowed to meet you, and no respectable woman should share a room with you. I reminded him that you were my friend and asked what he meant. He told me, openly, in front of everyone. It was dreadful! Why does being your friend ruin young men? That poor boy in the Guards killed himself. You were one of his closest friends. Then there was Sir Henry Ashton, who had to leave England with his reputation destroyed.”

I removed its covering, and a light breeze soon stirred it into flame. Taking note of this as well, I fashioned a fan from branches, with which I revived the embers whenever they were almost dead. At the next coming of night I discovered with delight that the fire furnished light as well as warmth. This element proved useful also in preparing my food: some scraps abandoned by the travellers had been roasted, and I found them far more appetising than the berries I plucked from the trees. I therefore attempted to cook my own provisions similarly, laying them upon the glowing coals. This treatment ruined the berries, but greatly improved the nuts and roots.

“Food grew scarce, however, and I often devoted an entire day to seeking, unsuccessfully, a handful of acorns to quiet my hunger. Accordingly I determined to leave the spot where I had until then resided and find another where my few needs might be met more readily. In making this departure I deeply regretted losing the fire, which chance had given me and which I had no knowledge of creating anew. For several hours I earnestly considered this obstacle, but at last had to abandon every attempt to overcome it. Drawing my cloak about me, I set off through the wood in the direction of the sinking sun. Three days passed in such wanderings before I finally reached open country. Heavy snow had fallen during the previous night, leaving all the fields uniformly white. The prospect was cheerless, and the cold, damp material spread over the earth chilled my feet.

“It was roughly seven in the morning, and I yearned for something to eat and a place of refuge. Presently I discerned a little hut upon a rise, plainly erected for a shepherd's use. Never having beheld such a thing, I studied its construction with considerable curiosity. The door stood open, and I went inside. An old man sat by a fire, preparing his morning meal over it. Hearing a sound, he turned; at the sight of me he screamed, fled the hut, and raced over the fields at a pace his feeble frame would hardly have suggested. Both his appearance, unlike any I had previously encountered, and his flight astonished me somewhat. But the hut itself delighted me. Neither rain nor snow could enter; its floor was dry. To me it seemed as perfect and heavenly a sanctuary as Pandæmonium must have seemed to the demons of hell after their torments in the fiery lake.”
